questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Let $S$ be a non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$. Consider the following statement:
p : There is a rational number $x \in \mathrm{ S}$ such that $x>0$.
Which of the following statements is the negation of the statement p?
options: There is a rational number $x \in \mathrm{ S}$ such that $x \leq 0$.
There is no rational number $x \in \mathrm{ S}$ such that $x \leq 0$.
$x \in \mathrm{ S}$ and $x \leq 0 \Rightarrow x$ is not a rational number.
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \text{ Given statement is } \\
& \\
& \exists x \in \mathrm{ S} \text{, such that } x>0 \\
& \therefore \quad \sim(\exists x \in \mathrm{ S}, \text{ such that } x>0) \\
& \equiv \forall x \in \mathrm{ S}, x \leq 0
\end{aligned}$
i.e., Every rational number $x \in S$ satisfies $x \leq 0$.

questions.q: If $\mathrm{A}=\{x, y, z\}, \mathrm{B}=\{1,2\}$, then the total number of relations from set $\mathrm{A}$ to set $\mathrm{B}$ are
questions.solution:
It is given that $A=\{x, y, z\}$ and $B=\{1,2\}.\therefore A \times B=\{(x, 1),(x, 2),(y, 1),(y, 2),(z, 1),(z, 2)\}$
Since $n(A \times B)=6$, the number of subsets of $A \times B$ is $2^{6}.$
Therefore, the number of relations from $A$ to $B$ is $2^{6}.$

questions.q: The chances to fail in Physics are $20 \%$ and the chances to fail in Mathematics are $10 \%.$ What are the chances to fail in at least one subject?
questions.solution:
Let $P(A)=\frac{20}{100}=\frac{1}{5}, P(B)=\frac{10}{100}=\frac{1}{10}$
Since, event are independent and we have to $\text{ find } \begin{aligned} P(A&\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A) \cdot P(B) \\
&=\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{10}\\
&=\frac{3}{10}-\frac{1}{50}=\frac{14}{50}=\frac{14}{50} \times100=28 \%
\end{aligned}
$
